title: Other Work
text:
How Representative Are Politically Active Social Media Users? A Descriptive Large-Scale Study of Danish Twitter Users
with Michael Bang Petersen and Stig Hebbelstrup Rye Rasmussen · in progress
Political debate on social media is often read as a reflection of public opinion, even though the people who produce it may not resemble the population at large. Linking a large sample of Danish Twitter users to population data, this descriptive study documents how the politically active social-media public differs from ordinary citizens.

title: Experiences of Administrative Burden
text: If the first agenda asks which demands are seen as legitimate, this one asks what those demands do to the citizens who face them. Administrative burdens — the learning, compliance, and psychological costs of dealing with the state — are consequential and unequally distributed. Here I study how citizens experience these costs, who bears them most heavily, and where common assumptions in the literature do not hold up to closer scrutiny.

title: Experiences of Administrative Burden
text:
Work in Progress


Personality as a Mechanism of Inequality in Experiences of Administrative Burdens
in progress · preprint
Experiences of administrative burden vary substantially across individuals, but the psychological sources of that variation are not well understood. This paper argues that two stable personality traits—conscientiousness and emotional stability—shape how citizens cope with administrative demands. Across two studies fielded in a pre-registered Danish survey, both traits consistently predict lower learning, compliance, and psychological costs, and match or exceed established predictors such as education, health, and financial scarcity. The paper received the Best Paper award in the Behavioural Public Administration Research Group at the 2026 ENPA Conference.


Færre valgsteder, færre vælgere? Valgstedslukninger og valgdeltagelse fra 2007-2026
with Lea Munksgaard Rubin · Politica, revise and resubmit
The number of polling places in Denmark has fallen markedly since the early 2000s, driven by decentralized municipal decisions rather than any central reform. Using panel data on all 98 municipalities across parliamentary, municipal, and European Parliament elections from 2007 to 2026, we estimate the effect of a municipality reducing its number of polling places with a two-way fixed-effects model. We find a small but significant negative effect on turnout, concentrated in second-order elections: largest for the European Parliament, smaller at municipal elections, and absent at parliamentary ones. Closures also increase the share of postal votes, so some voters compensate by voting by post rather than abstaining.

title: The Legitimacy of the State’s Demands
text:
The modern state constantly makes demands of its citizens, and people disagree about how far those demands should reasonably go. This agenda asks which demands citizens, frontline workers, and policymakers regard as legitimate and are willing to support — what the field calls burden tolerance. It speaks to the larger question my work revolves around: how demanding can a democratic state be while keeping the trust and legitimacy of those it serves?


Burden Without Backlash? Trust and Procedural Fairness in Response to Welfare Compliance Demands
with Frederik Godt · Policy Studies Journal, conditionally accepted, 2026
preprint
A common rationale for tough compliance demands in welfare programs is that, by signaling program integrity and guarding against fraud, they reassure the public and build trust in government. We test that rationale directly. The demands do raise citizens’ perceptions of procedural fairness, but this does not carry over into greater trust in government. The results question the case for using burdensome procedures to build legitimacy.


Do Justifications Affect Tolerance for Administrative Burdens? Evidence from a Survey-Experiment Among Policy Makers
with Steven van de Walle · Social Policy and Administration, 60(1): 12–26, 2026
Policymakers design the procedures that organize citizens’ encounters with the state, yet we know little about what makes them willing to impose burdens. Using a survey experiment among local politicians in Flanders, we show that policymakers become more tolerant of burdens when given a justification for them. Justifications that appeal to protecting public budgets are especially effective, and they work more strongly among right-wing than left-wing politicians.


Burden Tolerance: Developing a Validated Measurement Instrument across Seven Countries
with Martin Bækgaard and Donald Moynihan · Public Administration Review, 85(2): 519–546, 2025
Cumulative knowledge about burden tolerance has been held back by the absence of a validated way to measure it. Drawing on 12 surveys across seven countries, we develop and validate a compact four-item scale of people’s acceptance of state-imposed burdens. Tolerance varies widely across countries but follows consistent patterns: it is higher among men, the young, conservatives, and those who trust the state.


How Difficult Should It Be? Evidence of Burden Tolerance from a Nationally Representative Sample
with Pamela Herd and Donald Moynihan · Public Management Review, 25(11): 2053–2072, 2023
While research had begun to ask how policymakers and bureaucrats think about burdens, far less was known about the public’s own tolerance for them. Using a representative sample of US residents and the cases of Medicaid and SNAP, we find broad support for work requirements but weaker support for making benefits generally hard to access. Conservatives, those opposed to social policy, and higher-income respondents are more tolerant, while people with personal experience of welfare are markedly less so.

title: Teaching
text: I teach courses in public administration and policy evaluation at Aarhus University, at both undergraduate and graduate level. My teaching draws on research in public policy, administrative behaviour, and quantitative methods.

title: Teaching
text:
Supervision
I supervise master’s theses in public administration, public policy, and related areas. I have supervised 3 individual and 2 group theses (2025–2026), and served as internship supervisor for 7 students (2024–2026).
Students interested in thesis supervision in the areas of administrative burdens, citizen-state interactions, frontline workers, or political participation are welcome to reach out.

title: Aske Halling
text:
Assistant Professor · Aarhus University

I am an Assistant Professor at the Department of Political Science at Aarhus University. My research centers on a basic feature of the modern state: it constantly makes demands of its citizens — to document, to comply, to wait, and to prove they deserve help. I study these demands along three connected agendas: which demands citizens, frontline workers, and policymakers regard as legitimate; how the demands are experienced by the citizens who face them; and how fairly people are treated in citizen–state encounters.
I received my PhD from Aarhus University in 2023 and have published in journals such as Public Administration Review, Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory, and Public Administration. My work has been recognised with best paper awards at Politica (2024) and the ENPA Conference (2026).

title: Fairness and Discrimination in Citizen–State Encounters
text: The third agenda turns to how fairly people are treated in citizen–state encounters. Two directions of unequal treatment run through this work: whether frontline workers treat some citizens—the sick, or ethnic minorities—differently from others, and, less studied, whether citizens themselves discriminate against the frontline workers who serve them.

title: Fairness and Discrimination in Citizen–State Encounters
text:
Work in Progress


No Evidence of Ethnic Discrimination in Danish Caseworkers’ Sanctioning Intentions: A High-Powered, Preregistered Survey Experiment
with Julian Christensen, Frederik Godt, and Niels Bjørn Grund Petersen · Journal of Behavioral Public Administration, revise and resubmit
A recurring concern is that frontline caseworkers sanction ethnic-minority clients more readily than otherwise identical majority clients. This high-powered, pre-registered survey experiment tests for such discrimination in caseworkers’ stated sanctioning intentions. Contrary to common expectations, we find no evidence of it. The study adds a well-powered null result to a literature that has often relied on smaller, less conclusive designs.


“Everybody Should Be Able to Attend to Any Client, But…” – How Frontline Workers and Frontline Managers Interpret Citizens’ Differential Treatment of Staff
with Mathilde Cecchini and Benedicte Gronhoj · in progress
This qualitative project examines citizens’ discrimination against frontline workers from the staff’s own perspective. Drawing on interviews with frontline workers and managers, we ask how potentially discriminatory requests—a client asking not to be served by a particular staff member—are interpreted and handled on the frontline, and how workers experience being put in such situations.
